problem: Prior open-vocabulary navigation methods (VLMaps, CoW, CLIP-Fields, NLMap) handle explicit 'go to X' commands or short implicit ones, but struggle with long, conversational, implicit user queries. CLIP-based methods are limited to 77 tokens and encode all distracting content, and NLMap must first guess which objects to look for.
motivation: Natural human-robot interaction is conversational, and the target object is often never named. The observation is that an LLM can infer the user's intent better when it is told which objects actually exist in the scene, instead of hypothesizing objects blindly.
key_idea: Give an LLM a list of all objects detected in the scene during exploration, let it pick the object that best satisfies a conversational query, then look up that object's location in a spatial language index.
insight: Conditioning the LLM on a holistic list of detected scene objects beats having the LLM propose objects first (NLMap). The gap grows with query complexity: on conversational queries GPT-4 gives 1.20 m for CARTIER-ObjectDepth vs 2.11 m for NLMap and 2.35 m for the VLMaps baseline. A simple detector-bbox+depth index (ObjectDepth) beats the open-vocabulary VLMaps index (1.20 vs 1.70 m), so open-vocabulary mapping is not always needed. GPT-4 performance is similar across the three query types, suggesting the object detector, not LLM reasoning, is the bottleneck.
method: Environment exploration: the robot is teleoperated and collects RGBD frames with poses. Depth and 6-DoF pose give the best localization, but the ObjectViewpoint variant needs only a monocular camera and 2-DoF pose.
Object detection: the EVA detector (LVIS, 1204 classes) runs on all frames. Detections with confidence > 0.8 are compiled into a deduplicated list of objects in the scene.

Spatial language index: three variants map an object name to a position. VLMaps is a top-down grid of LSeg CLIP embeddings. ObjectDepth takes the frame with the largest bbox (with weak-perspective correction) and averages the depth points inside the bbox. ObjectViewpoint returns the robot position at that frame.

LLM query construction: a terse instruction prompt plus the user query and a comma-separated list of detected object types. The LLM is asked to pick the single most relevant object; there are no few-shot examples.

LLM querying: ChatGPT or GPT-4 at temperature 0, with minimal parsing of the answer. Because the LLM uses world knowledge, it can still point to a plausible location (e.g. the coffee machine for a 'tamper') when the target is not in the detector vocabulary.
Index lookup: VLMaps is queried via the CLIP embedding of the object name, taking the highest-similarity cell after dropping large embedding dimensions. The other two indices are read directly.

setting.backbone: ChatGPT and GPT-4 (frozen, prompted) + EVA object detector (pre-trained) + VLMaps/LSeg
setting.observation: RGB-D frames with 6-DoF pose from a teleoperated exploration trajectory (camera ~1.5 m high)
setting.action_space: predicts a target location in the map (goal position); no low-level control evaluated
setting.simulator: AI2Thor (7 scenes); real-world proof of concept with an Ohmni telepresence robot
setting.privileged: Simulator ground-truth pose during exploration; teleoperated exploration trajectory (pre-exploration of the environment)

numbers.eval_set_note: 7 AI2Thor scenes, 127 (query, scene) pairs per query type, 40 object types

numbers_note: Custom benchmark. Table 1 gives mean distance in meters (lower is better) for all variants. The object-match success rates appear only in a figure and are not given in the text.
results: CARTIER-ObjectDepth with GPT-4 reaches a mean distance of 1.20 m on conversational queries, versus 2.11 m for NLMap and 2.35 m for the VLMaps baseline; the abstract claims up to 42% more reliable parsing. The gap widens with query complexity. NLMap wins on object-match for explicit queries but loses on distance.
limitations: Small custom evaluation: 7 AI2Thor scenes and 127 pairs per query type, evaluated manually, with a simple closed-vocabulary detector that misses attributes (e.g. a dirty plate).
Only the 'go to' step (goal localization) is evaluated; there is no path planning or full navigation success metric, and it requires a prior exploration trajectory with GT pose in simulation.
Real-world validation is a single proof-of-concept example.
